MANILA, Philippines – Typhoon Rosal (Champi) continued to affect Batanes and other parts of Northern Luzon on Friday, October 23, even though it has spared the Philippines from landfall.
Rosal was last spotted 275 kilometers east northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, as of 4 am on Friday. The typhoon is moving northwest at only 15 kilometers per hour (km/h).
Its maximum sustained winds had weakened to 155 km/h on Thursday evening, October 22, while its gustiness eased to 190 km/h.
At its peak, Rosal was a super typhoon with maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in a bulletin issued at 5 am on Friday that Rosal is still bringing moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) to Batanes in the coming hours.

Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan, and Isabela may also continue to experience rain with gusty winds due to Rosal on Friday, while the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, the rest of Cagayan Valley, Ilocos Sur, La Union, and Aurora are likely to see scattered rain and thunderstorms caused by the typhoon.

PAGASA added that Rosal’s trough or extension is affecting Masbate, Palawan, the Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Basilan, and Tawi-Tawi. These areas could have scattered rain and thunderstorms as well.
Tropical cyclone wind signals also remain in effect in the following areas as of 5 am on Friday:
Gale-force winds (62 to 88 km/h), minor to moderate threat to life and property

blocks.text: Rosal may exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility by early Saturday morning, October 24. It entered PAR on Tuesday, October 20.
After leaving PAR, Rosal is likely to be downgraded to a severe tropical storm by Saturday morning, then weaken further into a tropical storm by Saturday evening.
Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.
The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com
